claims.text: The rapidly quenched starting alloy is a homogeneous, metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution with uniform elemental distribution.
Isothermal aging at service-relevant temperatures induces intermetallic precipitation in the Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
The precipitates include Mg-rich and other element-rich intermetallic compounds.
Intermetallic formation proceeds through diffusion-limited nucleation and growth.
Intermetallic precipitates form both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Intermetallic precipitation locally depletes the matrix of elements needed for protective oxide-film formation.
Local depletion of passivating elements weakens or disrupts the protective oxide film or scale.
Disruption of the protective oxide changes or degrades corrosion resistance.
Disruption of the protective oxide changes or degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aged samples will have a more heterogeneous microstructure and significantly more intermetallic precipitation than as-quenched samples.
Aging-induced precipitation will correlate with increased corrosion current density or altered passivation behavior.
Aging under mildly oxidizing conditions may accentuate the microstructural and performance changes.
The as-quenched alloy has intact protective surface oxides and superior corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The proposed mechanistic effects are most prominent between 350 and 550 °C.
Below 350 °C, atomic mobility may be too limited for the proposed transformation.
Above 550 °C, rapid degradation may obscure precipitation kinetics.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field says failure to observe either precipitation or corresponding performance changes would invalidate the hypothesis, whereas the formal falsification rule requires both no significant precipitation and no performance change. These are different logical criteria.
